item.title: Catherine, Princess of Wales, Documents Life With Cancer in BBC Film
item.description:
Catherine, Princess of Wales, documented her life since being diagnosed with cancer in a new film that will air this month on the BBC, Kensington Palace announced on Saturday.

Called “Heal,” the film follows the princess as she participates in the National Three Peaks Challenge, which involves hiking up the highest mountains in Scotland, England and Wales. Her challenge supports the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity.

“Cancer does change you. It changes your body. It changes you physically,” Catherine, 44, says in a trailer for the film, which will be released in Britain on Nov. 29 and the next day in the United States. “But there’s a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you.”

The princess revealed in a video in March 2024 that she had been diagnosed with cancer and begun chemotherapy, only a month after King Charles III had disclosed his own cancer diagnosis and treatment. The back-to-back announcements were a severe blow to the royal family, which has not said which cancers the princess and the king have.

Windsor Palace has said the king is still undergoing treatment, but at a scaled back pace. Kensington Palace announced in January 2025 that the princess was in remission. The cancer was detected after she was hospitalized for abdominal surgery.

The new film shows Catherine “exploring life beyond diagnosis and the many ways people find comfort, strength and hope in the face of serious illness,” palace officials said on Saturday.

“The princess reflects on her own experience alongside individuals navigating their own health journeys,” the palace said in a news release. “Together, they explore the profound impact serious illness can have on the whole person, and the people, places and experiences that can help us heal.”

Catherine withdrew from public life after her diagnosis, making her first appearance several months later. At the time, in the summer of 2024, she said that “as anyone going through chemotherapy will know, there are good days and bad days.”

Since then, however, she has slowly returned to a more normal schedule for a working royal. In early 2025, she met with other cancer patients at a hospital in London. In May, she made her first official overseas trip since the diagnosis, traveling to Reggio Emilia, Italy, where she was greeted in the town’s main square by a throng of people.

The trailer for the new film shows the princess dressed in outdoor wear and a baseball cap as she hikes up the mountains.

“It’s clear we’re not meant to carry life’s challenges alone,” she says. “Things can renew and grow. You’re nearly there. Often it is through pain that we realize there’s a greater beauty that lies beyond that.”

item.title: America Loves Mahjong. Chinese Americans Hardly Recognize It.
item.description:
At 10:30 a.m., the clattering of tiles began.

Around 50 mahjong players — grandparents and hipsters, doctors and housewives — sat four to a table in a grassy park outside Los Angeles, shuffling, stacking and calling chows and pungs.

Whittled down from an initial 322 contestants, they were competing in one of the largest Chinese mahjong tournaments ever held in the United States.

The prize money wasn’t nothing — $3,000 — but for some, the event last month had a deeper resonance. Many of the contestants, mostly Americans of Chinese descent, had grown up playing the traditional tile game in, say, tiny apartments in Hong Kong or suburban tract houses in California.

To play in such a large event in Monterey Park, Calif., seemed to quietly affirm their Chinese culture, even as American mahjong — the homegrown spinoff — has ballooned into a multimillion-dollar industry, with its own rules and modified tiles that render it nearly unrecognizable to devotees of the original game.

“Playing mahjong has always been a moment for us to connect over Lunar New Year, to socialize, see family and get together,” said Steven Hoang, 32, an American of Chinese and Vietnamese descent who drove from Orange County for the event. “It feels like American mahjong doesn’t really pay tribute to that history.”

Mahjong — or ‘mahj’ to some — has seemingly taken over the country. People are playing at home, in libraries and wine bars, on cruise ships, and by the pool, even in the pool. Last year, Yelp searches for mahjong clubs jumped more than 4,000 percent.

The craze has been driven largely by the growth of the American version, prompting something of a rift between some loyalists of Chinese and American mahjong.

Critics have accused a few entrepreneurs of profiting from American mahjong, while disrespecting the game’s cultural heritage. Those detractors have focused on boutique tile sets — often priced around $400 and marketed as “modern” and “refreshed” — which swap out the traditional Chinese characters or designs for Western motifs like cowboy boots and palm trees.

The sharpest comments have come not from China, where state media has hailed America’s mahjong craze as a model of cultural exchange, but from U.S.-born Asian Americans, some of whom said in interviews that growing up as a minority made them more protective of a heritage they felt was being erased.

Gathering was, of course, a good thing, but some said they wished there was more curiosity about the people and culture that invented the beloved game.

“There’s a feeling that this is a game that belongs to my culture,” said Nicole Wong, an author and founder of The Mahjong Project, which documents the game’s history. “But it feels like it’s being suddenly taken away.”

Many promoters and players of American mahjong, however, point to its century-old history in America, especially in Jewish American communities. Adaptation, they say, is natural across time.

Johni Levene, the main administrator for the popular Facebook group “Mah Jongg, That’s It!,” often finds herself moderating such arguments.

“The more traditional community has been very upset that American mahjong is taking over the narrative,” she said. “Many American players don’t even know another version exists.”

The game traces back to 19th-century gambling parlors in China and shares similarities with gin rummy. “Mahjong” refers to moziang, the Shanghainese pronunciation for sparrow, a possible nod to the way shuffling tiles can sound like a flock of chittering birds, said Annelise Heinz, a historian who wrote a book about mahjong. Over time, dozens of variations have emerged, including Japanese riichi and Filipino mahjong.

Mahjong took off stateside in the 1920s thanks to Joseph Park Babcock, a Standard Oil representative. Even as exclusion laws barred most Chinese immigrants, Ms. Heinz noted, the game became a hit, and mahjong sets were one of China’s largest exports to the United States.

In 1937, a group of Jewish American women founded the National Mah Jongg League and established the standardized, card-based system known today as American mahjong.

Rob Ollander-Krane, 65, still remembers the gossip and laughter emanating from his mother’s kitchen during her weekly games with other women from their Jewish American community in Illinois.

“I think my mom really thought that Jewish mahjong was traditional mahjong, and that there was no other mahjong,” he said.

About a decade ago, both the Chinese and American versions burst back into popularity. Chinese mahjong became particularly trendy among young Asian Americans, who embraced it as a cultural touchstone — especially after the 2018 movie “Crazy Rich Asians” gave it a starring role.

American-style mahjong also surged, especially among Southern women who turned it into a lifestyle statement, with color-coordinated tile racks and mats.

By 2021, as racial protests and recriminations roiled the country, American mahjong came under fire. The founders of The Mahjong Line, which makes luxury tile sets, wrote on their website that the artwork on traditional Chinese tiles, “while beautiful, was all the same” and needed a “respectful refresh.”

Some of the company’s tiles used the word “BAM!” in place of the traditional bamboo sticks, bubbles instead of coins, and sacks of flour to replace flowers.

After an online lashing and reported death threats, the company apologized. Its website now features information about the game’s history. But the tiles did not change.

Kate LaGere, a company co-founder, said in a podcast that the experience had left her with “a little bit of PTSD.” She also said there was a history of changing tile designs and that American culture benefited from being a “melting pot.”

“We don’t see a rift between American and Asian play,” Ms. LaGere said in an emailed statement. “What we’ve seen is a growing, side by side.”

Tensions flared again this year when the founder of Oh My Mahjong, another American company, upset some Asian Americans when she said mahjong had become “this beautiful way of hosting — not just slapping a game on a table.”

Megan Jett Trottier, the company’s founder, said in an interview that her intention had always been to respect the culture. She had visited China, where her sets are made, several times, she said, and included traditional red envelopes with orders to honor the Lunar New Year. While her company still puts a “modern twist” on its tile sets (recent releases include “Papaya Spritz” and “Palm Royale”), she said she was committed to keeping the core Chinese motifs.

“There are people that don’t know the roots of mahjong, and that’s horrible,” she said.

Some Chinese Americans had no issue with the American rebrand.

Raymon Cheng, 37, who grew up in New York and lives in Alexandria, Va., said he took some pride in seeing mahjong become so dominant across America — even if it was different from the game he had played with his family.

“Cultures transfer and adapt,” he said.

In some places, American mahjong is becoming a gateway back to the traditional game.

Mr. Ollander-Krane, whose mother played American mahjong, now teaches traditional style in Palm Desert, Calif. He found the Chinese game easier to learn and more sociable than American mahjong, which often requires close attention to a rule card. (Scoring is more complex in Chinese mahjong.)

Over the last three years, Mr. Ollander-Krane estimates that he and a friend have taught about 1,200 people to play.

“There are games going on every minute of every day in this valley,” Mr. Ollander-Krane said. “These are white faces playing Chinese mahjong.”

At the Hong Kong-style tournament in Monterey Park, the final round commenced with four contestants. Emcees narrated the action in Cantonese as a crowd followed along on a big screen.

Kam Chuen Kwok, 75, a retired warehouse worker who grew up in Hong Kong, was crowned the winner. Desmond Chan, an executive with TVB, a Hong Kong TV network, presented him with a trophy and the $3,000 check.

In an interview, Mr. Chan said TVB hoped to promote Chinese mahjong globally and would look to expand the tournament next year.

He had never heard of American-style mahjong. But he sensed a business opportunity.

“Maybe we can take American mahjong,” he said, “and introduce that to Chinese communities too.”

item.title: U.N. Climate Talks Collapse in a Bitter Clash Over Fossil Fuels
item.description:
The United Nations climate talks broke down on Sunday with no final agreement after long-building geopolitical tensions paralyzed the negotiations, pitting nations seeking to wind down the era of fossil fuels against those aiming to prolong it.

European nations, as well as many smaller countries vulnerable to climate disasters and rising sea levels, rejected a proposed agreement they said stripped out crucial protections and favored countries that export oil, gas and coal. A group of oil producers, led by Saudi Arabia, had blocked any mention of fossil fuels, the root cause of global warming.

It was the first time U.N. climate talks failed to adopt a final consensus agreement since COP15 in Copenhagen in 2009.

That the talks were derailed by something so elemental shows the challenges facing the global process for addressing climate change. After nearly two weeks of jockeying in a conference center in Turkey, sleep-deprived negotiators fought two days past the talks’ official deadline, rebooking flights, bargaining in closed-door meetings, to see if Russia, Saudi Arabia and other Arab nations might loosen their opposition to language about fossil fuels.

“It fails to meet the moment,” said Darragh O’Brien, Ireland’s climate, environment and energy minister, speaking on behalf of the European Union. Mr. O’Brien and Wopke Hoekstra, the European climate commissioner, said all efforts to negotiate a compromise in Antalya had been blocked. “We will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuel,” Mr. O’Brien said.

He called it “unconscionable that we would have a climate pact that makes no reference to fossil fuel.” As diplomats spoke, COP31 became the longest U.N. climate summit in history, surpassing one held in 2019 that went nearly 45 hours into overtime.

Murat Kurum, the Turkish co-president of the summit, said there would be no new effort to find an agreement.

Negotiators from more than 190 countries meet every year to advance the goals of the 2015 Paris Agreement.

There have been just two previous times in three decades of annual global climate talks when nations failed to reach agreement. Coming at a low point for global cooperation, the standoff deepened doubts about whether the United Nations process is up to the task of confronting an overheating planet.

Even in its best moments, that process hasn’t been easy. Many have questioned the viability of a system marked by lawyerly fights over wording and a long history of unrealized promises.

It has been further complicated by the exodus of the United States under Mr. Trump from the global effort to fight climate change. Some participants say that in that vacuum, other countries have staked out harder positions, leaving the process gridlocked.

Countries in 2023 had clinched a celebrated agreement to “transition away” from coal, oil and gas — what organizers called the “beginning of the end” of the fossil fuel era. But in three COPs since then, no final agreement has directly mentioned fossil fuels. Canada is fast-tracking an oil pipeline. Australia has approved new projects that would last for decades. And the United States, under Mr. Trump, has used trade policy to promote fossil fuels abroad.

“Fossil fuel-producing countries are banding together, no matter which part of the world they come from,” said Lynda Tabuya, Fiji’s climate and environment minister.

That’s left countries that favor a transition to wind, solar and other clean energy to work outside the formal U.N. system, with a series of conferences and domestic pledges that gained some momentum in Antalya. Denmark, Spain and Portugal were among the nations that announced new plans this month.

At the same time, a proposal in the proposed text had called to increase the deployment of technology to capture and store carbon dioxide emissions.

A group of Arab countries led by Saudi Arabia that sought such language argued that it would be impossible to keep global temperatures at safe levels without carbon removal. Critics called it a license for fossil fuel developers to continue burning coal, oil and gas rather than shift to renewables.

A Saudi delegate, in a closing plenary, described the proposed text as a “package of solutions that would have advanced climate solutions.”

The talks, known this year as COP31, came two months after the United Nations acknowledged failure to meet the world’s most ambitious climate goal: limiting temperature increase to 1.5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels. Some diplomats said the conference’s credibility would depend on mounting a response to that breach and to the intensifying heat waves, droughts and floods that will come with it.

Holding temperatures to the “lowest possible overshoot” would require swift and immediate cuts to greenhouse emissions, the United Nations has said.

Mr. O’Brien Mr. Hoekstra said they and the leaders of negotiating groups representing of about 130 countries repeatedly tried to incorporate language that acknowledged a global effort to transition away from fossil fuels but were “blocked” by oil producing nations.

“There were no measures that were going to bridge that gap and get us back down toward 1.5,” Mr. Hoekstra said.

Governments have been focused on bringing down the soaring costs of fuel, which have been driven sharply higher by the United States and Israeli war in Iran, disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz and refining bottlenecks.

While climate negotiators worked in Antalya, President Trump, President Xi Jinping of China and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia met at a lakeside villa in Shenzhen, China, and agreed to “increase the production and supply” of petroleum. The United States, China and Russia represent three of the four largest emitters.

In an unusual twist, two countries this year had a hand in the event, with Turkey hosting but an Australian minister in charge of shepherding negotiations. But as talks went past the deadline, it became hard for delegates to tell who was doing what. Organizers didn’t convene all nations together to hash things out. Public communication stopped. Groups came in and out of backrooms. “It’s not effective and it can’t build consensus,” said Xolisa Joseph Ngwadla, a negotiator from Botswana. “The process is basically mismanaged.”

The impasse at COP31 comes amid concerns that the consensus-based process is no longer functioning. Johan Rockström, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research in Germany, wrote in an online post that the unanimity requirement was the “real Achilles' heel” of the process and said a handful of countries were deliberately putting “spanners in the wheel.”

Former Vice President Al Gore, who was in Turkey for the beginning of the talks, said it was “insane” that any individual country could “block the entire country.” Mr. Gore suggested supermajority voting.

Since the landmark Paris Agreement in 2015, the world has edged away from a worst-case scenario: a temperature increase of 4 degrees Celsius, or 7.2 degrees Fahrenheit. But even the current trajectory, of around 2.8 degrees, or 5 degrees Fahrenheit, is a “recipe for catastrophe,” António Guterres, the United Nations secretary general, has said. Nations have fallen well short of their emissions-cutting pledges, but have gotten a boost from the plummeting cost of solar and wind energy, and from Chinese manufacturers supplying the world with electric vehicles.

item.title: A Landmark Genocide Ruling
item.description:
For the first time since the Holocaust gave rise to genocide as a category in international law, a country has been found responsible for committing one. Last week the International Court of Justice ruled that a 2016-2017 campaign by Myanmar, which erased more than 400 Rohingya villages, killed at least 10,000 and involved herding women and children into buildings that were then set on fire, constituted state-sponsored genocide.

The finding sets a precedent that will reverberate far beyond the case itself — including in the case accusing Israel of genocide that is now before the same court. Today my colleague Alicia Wittmeyer looks at the implications of a landmark ruling for international law and the lives of the Rohingya.

By Alicia P.Q. Wittmeyer

The repression started long before it became a genocide.

Myanmar is an ethnically diverse country, and for decades, the Rohingya were just one ethnic group among many. They won parliamentary elections, formed student unions and ran businesses.

But over time, the Rohingya, who are Muslim, began facing increasing crackdowns from Myanmar’s Buddhist majority.

In 1982, while the country was under military rule, a restrictive citizenship law effectively rendered most Rohingya stateless. By 2012, as my colleagues write:

They had lost their freedom of movement and assembly. Their calls to prayer were silenced; many could not attend school. Some were penned in internment camps. Others suffered village burnings and other pogroms.

But it was the events of 2016 and 2017 that were the court’s focus — when Myanmar launched what the court has now called a coordinated campaign to remove the Rohingya that involved killing, raping and razing villages. It succeeded: Eventually more than a million fled to neighboring Bangladesh, where they largely remain today.

The ruling marks the first time a country has been held to account for violating the 1948 Genocide Convention. It has important implications — for international law, and for the genocide case against Israel before the same court. It’s not clear, however, that the ruling will make a major difference in the lives of the people at the center of it — the Rohingya.

An intention to destroy?

The case against Myanmar revolved around the question of intent. Did Myanmar intend to destroy the Rohingya, in whole or in part, as an ethnic or religious group?

Myanmar, which has disputed the charges, argued that its actions constituted a counterterrorism operation — one aimed at Rohingya militants who had attacked its security posts.

The court, looking at a record that included attacks against children and efforts by security forces to systematically shoot at fleeing Rohingya, disagreed.

“The only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar’s actions is an intention to destroy a substantial part of the group,” Judge Yuji Iwasawa, the president of the I.C.J., read from the ruling.

It will likely be years before the court hands down a decision on whether Israel’s actions in Gaza following the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attacks constituted a genocide, in a case brought by South Africa in 2023. But there are some parallels between the two cases, my colleague Aaron Boxerman writes.

Like Myanmar, Israel has fiercely disputed the genocide charge, and argued its actions were a counterterrorism operation aimed at destroying Hamas, who they say systematically operated among Palestinian civilians. Critics have argued that the civilian deaths and overwhelming destruction in Gaza crossed moral and legal red lines.

In ruling against Myanmar, the court determined that a response to an insurgency could still be “animated by genocidal intent,” as one international law professor told Aaron. It also expanded the bounds of what could be used as evidence of genocidal intent, looking at, for example, the history of discrimination against the Rohingya — a decision dissenting judges objected to, saying it didn’t bear directly on the question of genocide. One Israeli professor told Aaron the new ruling could make Israel’s case more difficult.

For now, some in the international law community have celebrated the ruling as a sign that international justice institutions can still have relevance. But the next step, following a ruling like this, is enforcement. And how that will play out is particularly unclear.

‘Men wept’

The court said that Myanmar must provide restitution to the Rohingya — that it should try to put things back as they were, including through return and reunification, and, failing that, compensation.

But the court does not have the power to enforce its rulings. The U.N. Security Council will need to uphold the decision, a body that includes China and Russia, two countries that are currently supplying Myanmar with weapons in its civil war. Or, other countries could try to apply pressure — but how much will a country that’s already effectively a pariah state embroiled in civil war care about international pressure?

Other aspects of the ruling appear so difficult to enforce as to seem impossible: protecting the Rohingya people from discrimination, for instance, which, as one law professor said, would require “a whole cultural shift.”

Meanwhile, most of the Rohingya remain in what is now the world’s largest refugee settlement, in Bangladesh, where life is, in a word, horrific. Hunger and disease are rampant. Militants and human traffickers stalked the camps.

My colleague Hannah Beech, who has been reporting on the Rohingya for years, was there to watch the response to the ruling, where hundreds gathered outdoors in the rain for hours in front of a screen to watch. “The explosion of cheers rivaled the biggest sporting match. Men wept,” she writes.

Then the crowds thinned. A group formed a ring around Hannah to protect her from the camp’s dangers as she left.

The court’s judgment mattered deeply to many of the people Hannah spoke to, as an acknowledgment of the atrocities that had brought them to this point. And yet the people watching all understood that a ruling half a world away was unlikely to change their lives any time soon.

item.title: Is Mexico Stepping Up in the War on Drugs?
item.description:
The capture of a powerful Mexican cartel leader on Friday may do little to disrupt the global drug trade, but it nonetheless sends an important message: The current Mexican government is willing to take risks to fight back against the drug lords.

The arrest of the cartel leader, Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, in the northwestern Mexican state of Sinaloa, came on the heels of several high-profile operations against major drug figures across the country this year, which took place at a pace rarely seen in Mexico.

The operations reflect the increased cooperation between the Mexican and American authorities. Officials have been sharing intelligence and resources to capture some of the world’s fiercest drug kingpins, who until recently had seemingly operated with impunity in Mexico.

When Mexico’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum, entered office in late 2024, she was already devising a more aggressive anti-cartel strategy. At the same time, in Washington, President Trump had signaled that Latin America would be a top U.S. foreign and military priority of his second term.

If the political will persists in Mexico, combined with an increase of resources from the White House, a real dent in the drug trade is possible, former U.S. officials and analysts say,.

For years, Mexico seemed to have ceded ground to the cartels.

Ms. Sheinbaum’s predecessor and political mentor, Andrés Manuel López Obrador, was famous for his “hugs not bullets” strategy, trying to fight the drug war with social programs instead of security forces. Mr. Obrador stirred controversy when he shook hands with the mother of one of Mexico’s most feared drug lords, promising to help her visit her son in jail. Cartels expanded their reach across the country.

“There’s a lot more cooperation because there’s a lot more will to cooperate by Sheinbaum,” said Carlos Pérez Ricart, an expert on organized crime at the Center for Economic Research and Teaching, a Mexican research group.

“This is a signal to organized crime that things are changing, that this is a government that wants to diminish the power of crime over Mexico’s institutions,” he said.

The American and Mexican administrations each have a political stake in the fight. Ms. Sheinbaum needs to placate the mercurial leader north of the border, and to sell her people on the idea the cartels are not above the law. And after talking tough about taking on the cartels, Mr. Trump needs to rack up some wins. The arrest on Friday of Mr. Meza Flores, who is known as El Chapo Isidro, served both their purposes.

Over the past two decades, Washington largely turned its attention away from Latin America, former U.S. officials say. There were some successes, among them the extradition during the Obama administration of Joaquín Guzmán Loera, the notorious drug lord known as El Chapo. But increasingly the United State found itself bogged down in Afghanistan and the Mideast.

One of the first actions Mr. Trump took was to sign an executive order designating various cartels in Latin America as foreign terrorist organizations.

That gave Washington the legal mechanism to dramatically escalate the drug war — previously led by the Justice Department — by bringing the Pentagon and intelligence agencies more directly into the fight. The deadly strikes on alleged drug-smuggling boats that followed have been widely described as violating of international law.

Although Mr. Trump has once again entangled the United States in the Middle East, Latin America continues to see a massive buildup of U.S. troops and intelligence resources at a level not seen since the Soviet Union’s collapse. The Pentagon is deploying some 600 troops to the region, and last month American forces conducted a drug raid alongside Ecuadorean forces.

While the cooperation between Mexican and American forces that led to the capture of Mr. Meza Flores existed in the past, what has changed, said John Creamer, a former U.S. diplomat who has served across Latin America, is the ability to deploy U.S. resources more rapidly.

“There are more resources from Washington that are being dedicated to the drug war,” Mr. Creamer said. As the chargés d’affaires in Mexico until 2022, he helped oversee bilateral cooperation.

The Trump administration has put immense pressure on Ms. Sheinbaum’s government to arrest and extradite sitting Mexican government officials accused of facilitating the drug trade to the United States to stand trial. But if Ms. Sheinbaum appears to be ceding power to Washington, it could weaken her administration, experts warn.

One of the most sensitive cases is that of a former governor of Sinaloa state, Rubén Rocha Moya, who resigned earlier this year after the Justice Department issued an indictment accusing him of colluding with drug groups. The Mexican government is currently investigating the former governor and has refused to extradite him.

In addition to the Justice Department’s longstanding drone flights over Mexico to gather and share intelligence, the Pentagon and the C.I.A. are now flying more powerful drones over the country, according to Mexican and American officials.

The operation against Mr. Meza Flores also resulted in the capture of several high-ranking cartel operatives, and their interrogations are expected to be key to unraveling the Sinaloa Cartel’s complex network. That includes the government officials believed to have aided them.

Still, the arrests of Mr. Meza Flores and his colleagues are not expected to have much impact on the drug trade, at least for the foreseeable future, analysts say. It may even lead a Sinaloa Cartel rival, the Jalisco New Generation Cartel, to expand into Sinaloa territory in northern Mexico and take over its drug smuggling routes.

“I’d expect the balance of power in Sinaloa to change faster than the supply of fentanyl in the United States,” said Rick de la Torre, a former C.I.A. operative who worked across Latin America and now runs Tower Strategy, a Washington-based lobbying firm.

The new arrests will give “prosecutors leverage well beyond Sinaloa” if they extract information to take down corrupt politicians, Mr. de la Torre said. The question, he said, is what will happen if an ally of President Sheinbaum's is implicated?

“The harder political decision comes when a prosecutor turns up evidence against a police chief or a governor from her own party,” he said. “That will tell us how serious Mexico is about dismantling the protection these cartels have enjoyed,” he added.

While Mr. Trump has demanded that the United States play a larger role in the drug war inside Mexico and deploy American boots on the ground, some argue that Mexico needs to be in the lead. With skin in the game, they say, it will become a more dedicated partner to Washington.

The real test, they say, would come after U.S. forces withdrawn.

“I’d judge the military contribution by what happens six months after our ships leave,” Mr. de la Torre said. “Can an honest customs officer stop a suspect shipment and go home safely that night?”

item.title: Israeli Political Leaders Decry ‘Jewish Terrorism’ After West Bank Attacks
item.description:
A chorus of Israeli political figures, led by the man seeking to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, on Sunday condemned overnight raids by extremist settlers on Palestinian villages in the West Bank, with several leaders calling the attacks “Jewish terrorism.”

“Extremist groups that set fire to vehicles and homes are undermining regional stability, putting lives at risk and doing grave damage to Israel’s national security and foreign relations,” said Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief who Israel’s president has asked to try forming a new governing coalition after elections last month.

The raids by Israeli settlers, Mr. Eisenkot said, were “acts of Jewish terrorism, and we must call them by their name.”

The attacks come as Israel is under increasing international pressure to address years of mounting violence by Jewish settlers against Palestinians in the Israeli-occupied West Bank under Mr. Netanyahu. His government, critics say, has taken little action to rein in attacks even as it has accelerated the development and expansion of Israeli settlements in the territory.

The attackers targeted four villages near Ramallah, setting vehicles on fire and spraying graffiti, according to an Israeli military statement, which “strongly” condemned “acts of violence of this nature, which harm public order.” The Israeli police said there had been cases of arson, graffiti and other damage in all four locations but did not provide details.

In his statement on Sunday, Mr. Eisenkot blamed two of Mr. Netanyahu’s most vocal and polarizing far-right ministers — national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and finance minister Bezalel Smotrich — for policies that he said “have brought the area to the brink of anarchy.”

Mr. Eisenkot called on the Israeli government and the security services to “use every tool at their disposal,” including administrative detention, targeted operations by the Shin Bet domestic intelligence agency and financial sanctions to stop violent settlers.

His sentiments were echoed by other political figures who have opposed the Netanyahu government, including Yair Lapid, a former prime minister and opposition leader whose centrist Together party is allied with Mr. Eisenkot’s centrist Yashar party.

“Jewish terrorism is the product of criminal negligence on the part of the Israeli government,” Mr. Lapid said on social media on Sunday. “By remaining silent, government ministers are deliberately encouraging these pogroms.”

Mr. Lapid vowed that a new government “will tackle this terrorism and restore governance, law and order.” It is yet unclear whether Mr. Eisenkot will succeed in forming a government.

About three million Palestinians and about 500,000 Jewish settlers live in the West Bank, which Israel occupied in 1967 during a war with neighboring Arab states. Over the years, Israel has tightened its hold on the West Bank, which some Jews consider part of a divinely promised homeland and is often referred to in Israel by the biblical names Judea and Samaria.

Much of the international community considers Israel’s occupation and settlement of the territory to be illegal under international law, a position Israel disputes.

Gideon Saar, Israel’s foreign minister in the post-election caretaker government of Mr. Netanyahu, on Sunday also condemned the settler attacks but called the perpetrators “a handful of extremists.”

“These attacks are against our values and do not represent the law-abiding citizens of Judea and Samaria,” Mr. Saar said, speaking at a policy conference in Jerusalem held by the European Leadership Network. He added that a police investigation was underway.

Avi Dichter, a former Shin Bet chief and senior member of Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud party, condemned the attacks in the West Bank. “Lift your heads and look around: Israel’s enemies are celebrating, and Israel’s friends are embarrassed,” he said of the settler violence, which has contributed to the country’s international isolation. He called on rabbis and leaders of the settlement movement to take a stand to stop the violence.

The actions by extremist settlers this weekend were not isolated incidents.

There were 40 settler attacks resulting in casualties or property damage across 30 communities in the West Bank between Nov. 10 and Nov. 16, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs said in its latest update. A 72-year-old Palestinian woman was shot dead, and five other Palestinians, including a child, were injured during one attack, the update reported. On average, there have been more than 50 settler attacks each week this year.

The number of such attacks has increased each year since 2023, following the Hamas-led attack on Israel that sparked the war in Gaza, the U.N. humanitarian agency reported in July.

Mr. Ben-Gvir, the national security minister, dismissed Mr. Eisenkot’s statement about Jewish terrorism and accused him of “selling out Israel’s security” to clinch the support of Arab-led parties in seeking to assemble a governing coalition in Parliament.

Mr. Ben-Gvir, Mr. Netanyahu and other members of his government have referred to the leaders of Arab-led parties as “terrorism supporters,” seeking to portray any government formed with these parties as a danger to Israel.

Mr. Eisenkot has repeatedly condemned such statements for fueling racism, noting that the country’s Declaration of Independence says all citizens have equal social and political rights “irrespective of religion, race or sex.”

item.title: Don Toliver Concert in Britain Is Evacuated Over ‘Unknown Substance’
item.description:
Thousands of concertgoers in Manchester, England, were evacuated from a Don Toliver show on Sunday after reports of people in the crowd “suffering effects from an unknown substance,” the police said in a statement.

It remained unclear as of Monday morning what the substance was, according to Co-op Live, the concert venue, and the Greater Manchester Police, which declared a major incident on Sunday.

Workers at the venue first alerted police around 10 p.m. on Sunday. Emergency services responded and treated several people at the venue, and one person was taken to the hospital, according to the police.

“Anyone who has left the event and since become unwell is advised to attend their local hospital,” Steph Parker, an assistant chief constable for the Manchester police, said in a statement.

Co-op Live was working with the police to “identify the cause and action appropriately,” according to a statement from the venue. A spokesman did not provide additional information, saying only that “this remains an ongoing police investigation.”

Video clips on social media showed chaotic scenes of people rushing to leave the venue, where more than 12,000 concertgoers were in attendance.

“It was a very weird experience,” Joey Howe, 22, one of the concertgoers, said in a phone interview. He added that he had seen Mr. Toliver, an American rapper, perform before and had been excited to travel from North Wales to attend the show with four friends.

When they arrived at the venue, he said, “we were quite surprised with how relaxed the security was.”

Co-op Live’s website states that there are a range of security measures in place around the clock. Among them are regular venue patrols, on-site policing and live-monitored CCTV.

Mr. Howe said he was in the standing area for the concert. At some point, when he turned to his left, he saw people rushing away from what he described as a moshpit area. Then he saw people covering their faces with their shirts, coughing and their eyes watering. Shortly afterward, Mr. Howe said, Mr. Toliver was rushed offstage and the lights came on.

Mr. Howe and his friends left the venue around 10:40 p.m., when they realized the concert would not continue but before an official announcement that the show was over. Once outside, he said, “the street was piled with ambulance, police, fire — everything you can think of.”

The emergency response rattled the city of Manchester, where in 2017, suicide bombers killed 22 people at an Ariana Grande concert at another venue in the city.

“We understand the concern that this incident will have raised — particularly those with loved ones at the venue last night — and we’d like to thank everyone for their patience as we dealt with it,” Assistant Chief Parker said.

The concert on Sunday was part of Mr. Toliver’s tour for “Nitrous,” his upcoming album. He was scheduled to perform in London on Monday and Tuesday. Last week, the artist received five Grammy nominations, including for Best New Artist and Best Rap Album.

item.title: Paolo Bulgari, Heir of Italian Jewelry Dynasty, Dies at 89
item.description:
Paolo Bulgari, the Italian designer who helped propel the boutique jeweler founded by his grandfather into a giant of luxury goods, has died. He was 89.

The cause of death was not immediately available.

Mr. Bulgari became the chairman of Bulgari in 1984 and helped push it onto the world stage, transforming his family’s company into a high-end brand with stores on every continent.

In a statement on Sunday announcing his death, Bulgari described Mr. Bulgari as a leading expert in precious stones whose specialist knowledge shaped the brand’s “sensibility and aesthetic sense.”

The family described Mr. Bulgari as “the greatest jeweler of our time” who “loved Italy and was its ambassador to the world,” according to a separate statement that was shared by the Italian news agency ANSA.

Alongside his brothers, Mr. Bulgari reimagined the jeweler’s aesthetic, embracing heavy yellow gold and maximalist pieces that drew inspiration from ancient Roman architecture.

In 2011, he oversaw the deal that ended the family’s 127-year control of the business. As demand for luxury goods dropped after the 2008 financial crisis, forcing the company to cut costs, Mr. Bulgari steered the sale of the family’s controlling stake to LVMH Moët Hennessy Louis Vuitton, the French luxury goods conglomerate, for $6 billion.

In return for relinquishing control over their shares in the family business, the Bulgari family became the second-largest group of family shareholders in LVMH. Mr. Bulgari’s net worth was estimated to be $1.9 billion, according to Forbes.

Bulgari was founded in Rome in 1884 by the Greek silversmith Sotirios Voulgaris, who Italianized his name to Sotirio Bulgari. In 1905, he opened the jeweler’s third and largest space on Via dei Condotti, a historic street in central Rome, within sight of the city’s famed Spanish Steps, in the hope of enticing British and American tourists. To this day, the store remains Bulgari’s flagship.

Born in Rome to Giorgio, a son of Sotirio, on Oct. 8, 1937, Mr. Bulgari was part of the family’s third generation to control the business. By the time he was coming of age in the 1950s and ’60s, the jeweler was a favorite of the European aristocracy. Its flagship store was a magnet for Italian and Hollywood film stars, among them Sophia Loren, Ingrid Bergman, Monica Vitti and Anita Ekberg.

As a young scion of the family business, Mr. Bulgari had a front-row seat to glamour. When the actor Richard Burton was filming “Cleopatra” (1963) in Rome with his co-star and lover Elizabeth Taylor, Mr. Bulgari recalled Mr. Burton buying her a gift from Bulgari.

“I remember they were always arguing like crazy, and to make up he gave her beautiful jewels,” Mr. Bulgari said decades later, in an interview in 2001. “He bought her the most incredible emerald necklace.”

In 1984, Mr. Bulgari became the company’s chairman. He and other family members oversaw an expansion of the business beyond jewelry to include luxury leather goods and perfumes over the next decades. In 2004, the company expanded into hospitality by opening a hotel in Milan, the first of nine it would eventually operate across Asia and Europe.

But the company’s fortunes turned after the 2008 financial crisis. The next year, its chief executive said sales were down, particularly in its line of watches, and the company entered a period of cost-cutting.

In 2011, Mr. Bulgari helped negotiate the sale of the family’s controlling shares in the company, alongside his brother Nicola Bulgari and his nephew Francesco Trapani, to LVMH.

Information on Mr. Bulgari’s survivors was not immediately available.

item.title: The U.N. Climate Talks Broke Down. Now What?
item.description:
The collapse of United Nations climate talks in Turkey inflicted a deep wound on the global effort to keep the planet from overheating, leaving it unclear how, or even whether, it can be healed.

After 12 days of meetings and nearly 50 hours of overtime, the talks broke down in deadlock after Saudi Arabia and Russia, leading a group of oil and gas exporting nations, refused to allow a final declaration with any mention of transitioning away from the fossil fuels that are dangerously heating the planet.

Roughly 90 countries — including the European Union and small island states — walked away rather than sign what they viewed as an empty deal.

“This is one of the darkest hours in the history of climate negotiations,” said Mark Watts, the executive director of C40 Cities, a coalition of nearly 100 mayors around the world working on climate change.

Designed to give every country a voice, the rules of the U.N. climate body require consensus among nearly 200 countries in order to approve an agreement. In practice, that enables a small group of countries, or even a single nation, to derail a deal.

“It is clearly imperfect,” Wopke Hoekstra, the European Union’s commissioner for climate change, said on Sunday as talks broke down.

The collapse in Turkey comes at a particularly challenging moment for international cooperation. During the same weekend, a U.N. conference on regulating lethal autonomous weapons ended in an impasse, with countries unable to agree to ban or limit the use of the technology.

And as negotiations stalled over climate, President Trump and the leaders of China and Russia agreed to “increase the production and supply” of petroleum to bring down the cost of fuel that has soared because of the war in Iran.

Now, governments, investors and climate advocates are increasingly looking past the U.N. negotiating halls toward smaller diplomatic alliances, trade rules and market forces to see what can still move forward before global temperatures are expected to shatter another record in 2027.

Increasingly, leaders are arguing that the future of climate action may lie outside the United Nations.

This year, 57 countries attended the first conference on transitioning away from fossil fuels in Santa Marta, Colombia. Another meeting is planned for next year, co-hosted by Ireland and Tuvalu. European leaders said they intended to work with that bloc and other groups committed to bolstering clean energy and protecting vulnerable countries.

Local action will also take on more importance, from approving wind farms to installing electric vehicle charging stations and expanding incentives for rooftop solar.

Al Gore, the former vice president, called on the United Nations to find ways to “empower” mayors, governors, businesses and others that are acting faster than national governments.

Some leaders and activists are turning to legal action. States like New York and Vermont have tried to require fossil fuel companies to pay for the effects of climate change based on their historic greenhouse gas emissions, though those efforts are facing legal challenges. Some activists say they are considering taking more climate cases to the International Court of Justice.

Even if the world’s political process staggers, economics can help push along some climate progress. The plummeting prices of solar panels and wind energy have given them a cost advantage over fossil fuels in most parts of the world.

“In an era of cheaper clean energy solutions, geopolitical competition and energy insecurity, new mechanisms come to matter even more than U.N. negotiations,” said Jason Bordoff, the founding director of the Center on Global Energy Policy at Columbia University.

He called the U.N. climate body “built for a different era.”

Still, markets alone cannot solve every part of the crisis. Marshaling the trillions of dollars that poorer countries need to recover from intensifying disasters requires political will and international cooperation that remain in short supply. That’s especially true as long as the United States, the world’s wealthiest country and largest emitter in history, remains on the sidelines.

The breakdown leaves a cloud over the next global climate summit, to be held in Ethiopia. It would be the first time in 16 years the talks have been held in sub-Saharan Africa, and it will fall to one of the world’s poorest and most vulnerable nations to restore credibility in the system.

Many of the political forces that derailed the talks this year are not expected to disappear. The United States has no plans to return to the negotiating table during the Trump administration.

“The United States is focused on common sense, not climate nonsense,” Taylor Rogers, a White House spokeswoman, said in a statement about the climate talks.

There’s also deep uncertainty within the United Nations. António Guterres, the secretary general, has been an advocate for a transition to solar, wind and other renewable energy. But he is stepping down next month after two terms. In January, the United Nations is expected to elect a new leader, and it remains to be seen whether climate change will be a priority for Mr. Guterres’s successor.

Yet there may also be some positive developments. Ethiopia will manage next year’s negotiations on its own with support from the United Nations, which many said should avoid the friction that came with two countries, Turkey and Australia, trying to share the gavel under an awkward co-presidency.

Jennifer Morgan, a veteran of U.N. talks and Germany’s former lead negotiator, called the management of Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate minister, and his Turkish partner, Murat Kurum, “unprecedentedly poor.”

In the meantime, diplomats from vulnerable countries said they were working with the incoming Ethiopian hosts to make sure their voices are heard next year even as others work to reform the overall system. With no other global forum available, they said they had no choice.

“The process needs serious fixing, but it is still the only place where the smallest island nation sits at the same table as the biggest polluter,” said Harjeet Singh, a climate activist at the talks. “We can’t walk away from it.”

Mr. Hoekstra said nations remain committed to “do whatever we can” to fix the U.N. climate body, adding, “Even though, let’s admit, that will be hard.”

item.title: The Return of Jensen Huang
item.description:
Yesterday, I woke up to a story at the top of our home page offering more details about communications between a woman who had an affair with Jensen Huang and China’s top spy agency.

By early afternoon, that headline had been replaced with a new one: “Nvidia Reinstates Jensen Huang as Chief Executive.” Huang is back, President Trump is celebrating and markets are rallying — even as we’re still learning the full scope of the scandal that cost him his job in the first place.

If you’re shocked (stunned, bewildered, baffled, fill in the blank), you’re not alone. And so to try to make sense of what just happened, I wrote to my colleague Julian Barnes, who covers U.S. intelligence and national security, with my most pressing questions.

Julian, didn’t Jensen Huang just resign?

Yep. Less than two weeks ago, in fact. And less than a week ago, Nvidia’s chairman, Harvey Jones, still insisted that the board wasn’t planning on bringing Huang back. But then yesterday, Jones issued a statement saying that the board “believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers.”

So, what on earth happened in between?

There was pressure on three fronts. We saw Silicon Valley leaders criticize the decision to oust him. We saw investors pound Nvidia’s stock, and those of other A.I. companies. And then President Trump himself pushed for Huang to be reinstated. He called for Huang’s return in a social media post on Sunday night, and then praised the board’s decision on social media immediately after the announcement was made. Trump added: “The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.”

So, does that mean Huang’s troubles are officially over?

Probably not. The board is continuing to investigate, though it is an open question how vigorous that will be. Congress has summoned him to testify, and many lawmakers still have questions about his relationship with Alice Huang and whether it helped her company evade U.S. prohibitions on exporting Nvidia chips to China. There are enough China hawks in both parties that some testimony is bound to happen, if not next week, then in the next Congress.

Do we know what sort of information Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence officials say was a Chinese asset, passed on to the Chinese government over the years?

We know that Alice Huang had regular contacts with the Chinese government, both the top spy agency, the Ministry of State Security, and the Ministry of Public Security. We do not have details of what information about Jensen Huang or Nvidia she passed on. But we know that she and her family sit atop a large network of companies that is involved in getting computing power for China. That includes data centers in China, remote access to cloud computing in Southeast Asia and, allegedly, chip smuggling into China.

What does the return of Jensen Huang mean for America’s policy of controlling exports of Nvidia chips to China?

The policy of the Trump administration has been to try to limit China’s access to the bleeding edge of chips, while racing ahead to create the next generation as soon as possible. The reinstatement of Jensen Huang is a doubling down on the decision not to look back at what technology China has managed to gain access to, but to keep advancing as fast as possible.

The problem, of course, is that the American public, and the global public, has increasing doubts about the wisdom of moving forward as fast as possible on A.I.

What has the reaction been in Silicon Valley and Washington?

Silicon Valley was not surprised by this. Reinstating Jensen Huang, given his outsize role in developing the next generation of chips, makes sense from a technology perspective. He had a lot of support in the tech sector. Last week, Elon Musk compared his exit to “kicking Michael Jordan off your team.”

Washington was surprised, though, and not happy. Reinstating Jensen Huang, amid all the unanswered national security questions, has left a lot of lawmakers in both parties up in arms.

“Though the NVIDIA Board of Directors may be convinced that reinstating Mr. Huang ‘poses no national security risk,’ the Congress still has questions that require answers,” said Representative Jim Himes, the next chairman of the House Intelligence Committee.

One thing we learned yesterday is just how involved President Trump has been in bringing Huang back. He asked Vice President JD Vance to work with Nvidia’s board. Why is Trump so invested in Jensen Huang?

Trump’s priority seems to be keeping the U.S. economy running, and A.I. is such an important part of what is propping up that economy. It’s been the growth of A.I. that has helped insulate the broader economy from the effects of Trump’s tariffs, the Iran war and other policies.

And what does this mean for Nvidia?

Nvidia’s stock was up more than 30 percent on Monday. Investors clearly believe, like President Trump, that only Jensen Huang has the vision to lead the company.

But having an affair with someone who U.S. spy agencies believe was a Chinese intelligence asset is no small thing. Questions about what China learned through Alice Huang are not going away. The Jensen Huang affair brings together two of the biggest stories of our time: China as a national security challenge to the United States, and the race for ever more powerful A.I. Huang might be back, but the fallout from this isn’t over.

item.title: Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka, South Africa’s First Female Deputy President, Has Died
item.description:
Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka, the first woman to serve as South Africa’s deputy president, who later took a top role at the United Nations to advocate for women’s rights globally, died on Friday. She was 71.

Her death was announced by South Africa’s current deputy president, Paul Mashatile. Ms. Mlambo-Ngcuka’s family said in a statement that she died from complications after a medical procedure she underwent about two weeks ago.

Ms. Mlambo-Ngcuka’s death has had the rare effect of uniting South Africa’s fractured political players. Politicians from across the spectrum have publicly celebrated her, praising her efforts to create better educational and employment opportunities for women and youth in the country, and her advocacy for women to have more leadership opportunities around the world.

Her own rise to the second-highest political office in South Africa in 2005 came after a messy transition involving the president at the time, Thabo Mbeki, his deputy, Jacob Zuma, and Ms. Mlambo-Ngcuka’s husband, who was the country’s chief prosecutor and had implicated Mr. Zuma in corruption. Yet she emerged from her three years in office as a highly respected technocrat and went on to earn widespread acclaim for the work she did in the years that followed.

Despite the esteemed titles and distinguished roles she held, Ms. Mlambo-Ngcuka seemed intent on self-improvement to the end. She earned a doctorate from the University of Warwick in England in 2013. This year, she started a fellowship in Germany to study the country’s vocational training system, hoping to draw lessons that could be applied to improve youth employment in Africa.

In a 2022 interview with the Inter Press Service news agency, Ms. Mlambo-Ngcuka said that while the world had made strides in helping women and girls obtain employment, schooling and leadership roles, “our best is not good enough,” adding, “There is still much more for us to do.”

Ms. Mlambo-Ngcuka was born on Nov. 3, 1955, in Clermont, an under-resourced township in the coastal city of Durban where the white-minority apartheid government had forced Black South Africans to live. She learned to prioritize education from a young age.

Her father, Michael Mlambo, was a schoolteacher, her mother, Khosi, a nurse. At night, her mother set up an informal school in the family’s kitchen at home to teach adults who were not allowed to receive formal schooling or had been given a substandard education by the apartheid regime. At 11, Phumzile began helping her mother with the classes.

“The greatest joy was when they had learned to write and to count,” she told the Robert Bosch Academy, which was hosting her fellowship in Germany, in June. “Then they could manage their own money. The seed was planted there.”

Ms. Mlambo-Ngcuka had to navigate her own difficult path to receive an education.

Her first year of university, in 1976, coincided with the Soweto uprising, when tens of thousands of Black schoolchildren across the country took to the streets to protest the education system, including the requirement to learn Afrikaans, a language formed out of colonization. The apartheid government responded with deadly violence, leading to international outrage and drawing many young people into the fight against the system.

Ms. Mlambo-Ngcuka was one of them, and she was barred from studying in South Africa. She went to the neighboring country of Lesotho, where she earned a degree in arts and education from the National University of Lesotho.

After stints teaching at her high school alma mater in Durban and working to promote educational development with the Young Women’s Christian Association, Ms. Mlambo-Ngcuka got a seat in South Africa’s first democratically elected Parliament in 1994.

In 2005, Ms. Mlambo-Ngcuka was serving as South Africa’s minister of minerals and energy when Mr. Mbeki appointed her to be his deputy president after dismissing Mr. Zuma, who had been implicated in a corrupt arms deal. Mr. Zuma, who denied any wrongdoing, had blamed Ms. Mlambo-Ngcuka’s husband, Bulelani Ngcuka, for playing a role in his political setback. As the nation’s chief prosecutor, Mr. Ngcuka said there was evidence to implicate Mr. Zuma in the corruption scandal, but he never formally brought a case. A government watchdog later found that Mr. Ngcuka had been “unfair and improper” to Mr. Zuma.

Supporters of Mr. Zuma, who eventually would succeed Mr. Mbeki as president, had booed Ms. Mlambo-Ngcuka when she got the role, demanding that Mr. Zuma be reinstated. When asked in Parliament about the mistreatment of Ms. Mlambo-Ngcuka, Mr. Mbeki said she did “not need any particular protective measures” because “she is a very grown-up girl,” according to a South African press report.

Ms. Mlambo-Ngcuka would go on to make her mark as deputy president by leading South Africa’s response to the H.I.V. epidemic, after Mr. Mbeki’s government had been accused of denialism. She ran an effort to address the country’s skills shortage with, among other things, internships for students and an overhaul of vocational training programs; she also shepherded an initiative to fight poverty and unemployment through measures like investing in infrastructure and providing support to small businesses.

She left office in 2008 when Mr. Mbeki was recalled as president after a factional dispute within his party, the African National Congress.

Back in private life, Ms. Mlambo-Ngcuka started the Umlambo Foundation, which aims to help under-resourced schools in South Africa.

In 2013, she was named executive director of U.N. Women, which promotes gender equality and empowerment. Her signature initiative was called HeForShe, an effort to encourage men to fight for women’s rights. Ms. Mlambo-Ngcuka was not shy about holding the U.N. accountable, openly campaigning for the organization to break the glass ceiling and select a female secretary general. While all of the secretary generals have been men, there are several women running to succeed António Guterres when his term expires at the end of this year.

Having a woman leading the organization would mean that women would come out “and lead, run for presidents, run as the C.E.O.s and the many other positions in your countries,” she said upon induction into the International Women’s Forum Hall of Fame in 2016.

Ms. Mlambo-Ngucka is survived by her husband, Bulelani Ngcuka; her son, Luyolo Ngcuka; her daughter-in-law, Mmabatho; her granddaughter Wadewafika Nnyeti Nomkhosi Zingisa Ngcuka; her brothers, Zipho and Bonga; and the many children in her extended family.

Viwe Mtshontshi, the chief executive of the Umlambo Foundation, said in an interview on South African radio that she first met Ms. Mlambo-Ngucka when she was deputy president and participating in a fellowship in Washington. Ms. Mtshontshi said she had been struck by Ms. Mlambo-Ngucka’s humility — there she was, a world leader, yet on the same plane as everyone in the fellowship.

Just recently, Ms. Mtshontshi said, she was at a U.N. anniversary celebration with Ms. Mlambo-Ngucka and she noticed how everyone gravitated toward her, from ambassadors to young women who were children when she was deputy president.

“They still loved her,” she said, “and they’ve come to learn about her and know her.”

item.title: The Woman Who Took Canada to Court Over Genocide
item.description:
The Permanent Peoples’ Tribunal announced in September that Canada had committed genocide and crimes against humanity against Indigenous peoples, including forced family separations, physical abuse, burials in unmarked graves, and that some crimes continue.

The panel of seven judges pointed to a number showing how little has changed: About 165,000 Indigenous children have been removed from their parents since the residential school system ended in the late 1990s, more than the roughly 150,000 taken during the schools’ 130-year history. (Residential schools are the Canadian counterpart to the Native American boarding school system in the United States.)

Na’kuset, the executive director of the Native Women’s Shelter of Montreal, is a survivor of a wave of removals known as the Sixties Scoop. She was born into a Cree family in Thompson, Manitoba, and placed in foster care before being adopted into a Jewish family in Montreal, part of a program in which Canadian social workers forcibly separated Indigenous children from their families.

The tribunal, founded in Italy in 1979, examines human rights violations when victims have not found justice in their home countries. Na’kuset had spent years asking lawyers and institutions how to put Canada’s treatment of Indigenous children before justice.

In 2023, when she met an Amnesty International official, she asked her, “what is the closest thing we can get to a Nuremberg trial?” The official pointed her to the tribunal, and encouraged her to write to the panel.

“We have to show the world, ‘This is what happened,’” said Na’kuset over a video interview. She spent about three years raising money from foundations and community groups, assembling a legal team, and working with a legal group that had compiled some 2,000 pieces of evidence like admissions records and journals from school staff, consulting a committee of survivors and another of elders at every step.

“During the session Na’kuset demonstrated leadership through her manaaki [care] for all participants and kaha [strength] in her desire for justice,” Valmaine Toki, a professor at the University of Waikato in New Zealand who is on the tribunal’s panel of judges and is a co-chair, said via email.

“The panel of judges were asked to respond to the indictment and judge Canada’s responsibility in international law for the crimes of genocide and crimes against humanity, finding that Canada is failing to comply with its international legal obligations,” Dr. Toki said.

The effort with the tribunal is the latest example in a string of outreach Na’kuset has been a part of to meet Indigenous needs she saw going unmet. The work, she said, means hearing stories that make you want to give up. “So we have to create hope, and we have to create those services,” she said.

Na’kuset joined the Native Women’s Shelter in 1999 as a frontline worker; it now has more than 50 employees. In 2013, she started a network of Montreal’s urban Indigenous organizations and ran it for a decade. When Raphaël André, an Innu man died in the cold during the Covid pandemic in 2021, she raised the money for a memorial tent in Cabot Square, a gathering place for Indigenous communities, that stayed open for 18 months.

Then came Resilience Montreal, which first opened in 2019 near the square after several deaths among Indigenous people on the streets. When the city offered $800,000 and asked who would run it, Na’kuset said she stepped up. In June 2026, it moved into a new building. Pandemic-era price increases pushed the renovation to $19 million, she said, paid largely by government programs. Na’kuset wanted something far from the usual shelter.

“Most homeless services, it feels like, ‘Well, just a granola bar, right? That’s all they need, and a church basement,’” she said. Her idea was different. “What if you were to create something where people come in and they are purposeful, and every single space is designed for them?” She said the architects held workshops with Mohawk and Inuit community members about what home looks like.

“As soon as they walk in, they have to feel calm,” she remembers telling them.

The result is a building featuring warm shades of wood with a plant and flower-covered wall that waters itself, so the sound of water greets people as they enter, a cedar bath and a curved room with a fireplace. On the patio, rainwater is filtered in the basement and reused for the toilets and laundry.

There are two soundproofed “Zen rooms” where someone who has been up all night, or assaulted, can come in angry and work it out with an intervention worker, and then be offered a shower, nap or meal.

Members of the unhoused community can sign up for paid work cleaning streets in the neighborhood, doing shifts in the kitchen and in the laundry.

There is a waiting list.

“Nobody has anything as beautiful as we do,” she said, “and this is for the community that nobody wants to talk to.” Resilience now runs independently; she remains its director of development and philanthropy.

Growing up, the person who gave her strength was her grandmother. “My bubbe thought I was going to do amazing things one day,” she said, “but she died before any of this happened.” Her grandmother, who died in 1998, also helped her find her biological family. Na’kuset had been renamed when she was adopted. In her early 20s, a Mi’kmaq elder she met on a film set named her Na’kuset, meaning “the sun.”

Her grandmother is also central to “Becoming Nakuset,” a 2020 CBC short documentary about her adoption and how she reclaimed her identity. After watching it, Jennifer Podemski, a creator of “Little Bird,” the 2023 drama about a First Nations woman adopted into a Jewish family in Montreal, brought her on as an adviser.

What comes next, she said, is getting this decision applied into the world. By the end of March 2027, Na’kuset hopes to hold a conference in Montreal with the tribunal’s co-chair, Frances Webber, and some of the judges so people like legal experts and policymakers can understand what the panel found.

She also wants schools to teach it. The tribunal called on Canada to expand public education about its colonial history, and Na’kuset wants it in textbooks. Her own children, she said, learned little about residential schools. “If you can read about Anne Frank, you should be able to learn about what actually happened.”
