item.title: China Fears A.I. Could Give the U.S. an Edge in Nuclear Rivalry
item.description:
When Xi Jinping, the Chinese leader, set about expanding China’s nuclear forces a decade ago, his goal was to ensure that enough missiles could survive an initial attack so Beijing could deliver a devastating counterattack.

That ability to withstand a strike and hit back would deter any enemy from risking nuclear blackmail or war against China in the first place, Chinese strategists have said.

But now, researchers in the Chinese military worry that American advances in artificial intelligence could weaken Beijing’s nuclear hand in a crisis or conflict. They have been warning that artificial intelligence could make it easier for U.S. forces to find and wipe out Chinese nuclear missiles, giving Washington a menacing advantage.

The worries over A.I. complicate the growing nuclear tensions between Washington and Beijing, and could make China more reluctant to consider limits to its smaller arsenal. At a summit on Thursday, Mr. Xi, President Trump and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia spoke of reducing nuclear risks. But Mr. Xi has shown no interest in Mr. Trump’s calls for China to join arms control commitments.

A review of more than 100 recent studies by Chinese civilian and military researchers, as well as interviews with experts and former U.S. officials, points to a deep wariness in China about the American pursuit of A.I. in nuclear systems. At the same time, Chinese military institutes are also exploring how A.I. could make Chinese missiles harder to detect and knock from the sky.

China, the United States and Russia use radars, satellites and sensors to monitor each other’s nuclear weapons. Breakthroughs in A.I. could help create technology to detect, track and strike nuclear weapons more quickly and accurately. Experts in China worry that it could lag the United States in applying such advances.

A study from China’s top military institute described a scenario in which artificial intelligence accelerated U.S. actions in a crisis to mere moments, potentially overwhelming slower rivals.

“By embedding A.I. and other technologies into nuclear decision-making systems, the United States could compress the decision-making process from the traditional 15 to 30 minutes to 90 seconds or less, drastically increasing the speed of response,” two researchers from the Academy of Military Science in Beijing wrote in an overview of global nuclear trends published several months ago.

China has about 620 nuclear warheads that could be delivered by land- or submarine-based missiles, or by bombers, the Federation of American Scientists estimates. China’s arsenal is widely forecast to grow to about 1,000 warheads by 2030. (The United States and Russia each have around 1,800 nuclear warheads deployed for missiles and bombers, with thousands more stockpiled.)

China fears that A.I. advances could enable the United States “to rapidly engage in strikes as soon as something pops out from a hiding spot or mobilizes,” said Gerald C. Brown, a former analyst with the State Department who studies China’s nuclear strategy. “Basically, in their view, it could make survivability a lot more difficult.”

China’s missile force is closely watching the U.S. Strategic Command, which controls nuclear missiles and has said that it wants to use A.I. to enhance “decision-making capabilities.” Chinese military analysts are also studying how American conventional forces use A.I. to coordinate operations and pick targets.

The U.S. edge in making advanced chips is adding to Chinese concerns that the United States can move faster to incorporate A.I. into its military, including in nuclear-related systems, said Jacob Stokes, a senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security in Washington.

Official history reinforces China’s anxieties. Chinese military officers studied the Korean War and crises over Taiwan in the 1950s, when the United States signaled that it could drop atomic bombs on Mao Zedong’s forces, which then had no nuclear weapons, said Mr. Brown, now an international affairs fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations.

China has already been diversifying its nuclear weapons to enhance their “survivability.”

In July, it held a test launch of a long-range missile from a submarine, showing its intention to create an undersea nuclear deterrent that could be harder for the United States to detect and destroy. China has also built about 320 launch silos in its northern deserts, which could make it harder for an enemy to determine which ones hold nuclear-armed missiles and knock them all out with precision strikes.

But Chinese experts now warn that breakthroughs in military A.I. could help the United States overcome China’s efforts to protect its arsenal and, in an extreme case, could tempt Washington to attempt a crippling first strike against those forces.

“I believe these risks weigh heavily in China’s strategic considerations,” Sun Chenghao, a senior fellow at the Center for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University in Beijing, wrote in emailed answers to questions.

“What China needs to assess is whether, under extreme circumstances, the U.S. might rely on A.I. reconnaissance, precision strikes and missile defense to weaken China’s capabilities to launch nuclear retaliation after an attack,” he wrote.

China’s leaders appear determined not to fall too far behind. In July, Mr. Xi held a meeting of senior officials to study the military implications of A.I. and other technological advances. He demanded steady progress toward their deployment.

In China, there is “great optimism that A.I. is the tool that is going to allow you to finally catch up to or surpass the United States militarily,” said Sam Bresnick, a research fellow at the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University.

Studies published by China’s Rocket Force, which controls most of its nuclear missiles, show a wide interest in A.I.

One study involving a Rocket Force scientist published last year examined how A.I.-enabled “deep reinforcement learning” could help hypersonic glide vehicles — weapons designed to dodge and weave as they approach their targets — better evade missile defenses.

The researchers simulated millions of possible flight paths to train an A.I. system to guide a hypersonic vehicle in flight. They used no-fly zones around Alaska as real-life examples of the challenges a hypersonic weapon might encounter, and test if A.I. could help the weapon navigate the defenses.

In another study, Rocket Force scientists used computer simulations to model how A.I. could help a ballistic missile get back on course after swerving to evade high-speed interceptors. An A.I.-assisted autopilot could calculate when to fire steering thrusters, secondary rocket engines that help change direction, while conserving fuel.

China should “apply cutting-edge technologies such as artificial intelligence and hypersonics, strengthening deployment of forces, and improving their survivability and retaliatory capabilities,” five scholars from a Rocket Force university wrote in a paper published this year that examined other countries’ nuclear exercises.

But even some researchers in the People’s Liberation Army have warned against rushing to introduce the technology in nuclear weapons systems.

In the most dire projections, rogue A.I.-generated internet viruses could commandeer nuclear weapons controls, disabling or launching the weapons.

But short of that, A.I. could incorporate and magnify false data, leading to dangerous, even disastrous, errors in crisis decision-making. Commanders could put too much trust in A.I.-generated conclusions or advice, experts say. Chinese studies have pointed to U.S. battlefield errors in conventional wars that they say reflect too much faith in automated targeting.

Erroneous information magnified through A.I. creates “enormous decision-making risks,” researchers from China’s National University of Defense Technology and the Academy of Military Sciences wrote in a study this year. “This is becoming the core obstacle to its deep application in the highly serious, high-risk field of command and control.”

Nuclear weapons systems have long contained high levels of automation to ensure accuracy, speed and security. But A.I. advances could reduce the role of human oversight in ways that can be dangerous during a fast-moving crisis, said Philip Reiner, the chief executive officer of the Institute for Security and Technology, a California-based group based that examines the implications of A.I. for nuclear weapons security and stability.

“This is a technology that is moving faster than anything any human has ever seen before,” he said of advanced A.I. “Nobody’s turning launch decisions over to A.I., but everything that tells you whether you should launch is now going to be shaped by A.I. And so, does that make it riskier? Yes.”

Yet even as the need for safeguards has become greater, the United States and China have made little progress in discussing them. Mr. Xi agreed with then-President Biden in 2024 to maintain human control over the decision to use nuclear weapons, but no official talks on the issue have followed. Mr. Xi, Mr. Trump and Mr. Putin did not mention the role of A.I. in nuclear weapons during their summit last week.

“Right now, there’s a lot of attention on the risks that A.I. is going to cause which could kill us all, but it’s abstract. Well, it has to have a mechanism,” said Melanie Sisson, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution who has discussed nuclear arms and A.I. with Chinese researchers. “Nuclear weapons are probably one of the most likely mechanisms. That’s why it’s so urgent.”

item.title: The Americas’ Longest War, and 10 Years of an Unfinished Peace
item.description:
A decade ago, the largest guerrilla group in Latin America laid down its arms, ending the longest-running war in the hemisphere.

Nearly half a million people had died. The violence had touched almost every aspect of society. The world’s eyes turned to Colombia as an example that peace was possible.

Today, the legacy of the accord is decidedly mixed.

The country’s main rebel group disbanded. But Colombia’s conflicts and criminal economies have only multiplied, fueling new cycles of violence.

Supported by

in photos

The conflict between Colombia’s government and a leftist rebel group ended in a historic 2016 accord. But Colombia is still waiting for true peace.

Photographs by Federico Rios

Written by Federico Rios and Julie Turkewitz

Julie Turkewitz has covered Colombia for the last seven years as the Andes bureau chief, and Federico Rios for the last 15, as a photographer.

The president called it “a common hunger” — peace.

On Nov. 24, 2016, the world watched as Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos signed an accord with the country’s largest insurgency, the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia. The agreement with the FARC ended a war that had lasted generations, dominated the regional security agenda and left millions of victims of kidnapping, disappearance and other abuse.

“Our dear Colombia,” Mr. Santos said, would no longer be “trapped in this labyrinth of violence.”

Thirteen thousand FARC fighters laid down their arms and the government pledged to address the root causes of the war, expand social programs, eliminate the illicit drug industry and establish a framework for truth and reconciliation.

Now, as Colombia marks the 10th anniversary of that deal, there is neither complete victory to celebrate nor absolute failure to mourn. Instead, Colombia has learned to live with a peace that is partial and uneven, a mix of real achievements and half-kept promises.

1960s

FARC fighters training at a camp in the jungle. The group’s origins trace back to the 1940s, when rural workers formed self-defense communities to resist state-backed violence, which morphed into a Communist insurgency by the mid-1960s.

1998

The bodies of Colombian soldiers killed during clashes with FARC rebels in the southern region of El Caguán.

2003

The FARC bombed El Nogal, an upscale social and business club in Bogotá. At least 32 people were killed in one of the deadliest urban attacks in the country’s history, solidifying public support for the military campaign of the conservative president Álvaro Uribe.

The deal led to one of the largest reductions in violence in modern Colombian history, measured in lives affected by displacement, massacres and homicides. But today, domestic support for the accord is at its lowest level since the signing. The country’s newly elected right-wing president, Abelardo De La Espriella, has criticized the deal and promised to dismantle it, and the country’s conflicts and criminal economies have only multiplied, fueling new cycles of violence.

Some Colombians see the country’s security problems as evidence of the deal’s failure; others say the violence is precisely why it must be kept in place — it is the hard-won framework needed to tackle deeply entrenched problems.

“We have a serious and comprehensive road map to close the gaps that fuel violence,” said Mr. Santos, who won the Nobel Peace Prize for his role in the deal. “That is why Colombia must continue moving forward with the implementation.”

2007

Íngrid Betancourt, a Colombian senator, was kidnapped by the FARC in 2002, while campaigning for the presidency, and held for over six years. Her rescue by the Colombian army marked the beginning of the FARC’s military decline ahead of the 2016 peace talks.

2010

A soldier wounded by a FARC land mine being airlifted by a helicopter from the jungle.

2012

A child soldier from the FARC’s Sixth Front with fellow guerrillas after an army ambush in the western mountains of Jambaló. Human rights groups have documented that thousands of minors, some as young as 9, were forcibly recruited into the FARC’s ranks.

As journalists working for The New York Times, we have documented this rocky path between peace and war, repeatedly visiting the nation’s most remote corners.

Colombia has long been an unequal country; in the 1960s the FARC sought to resolve that with guns, creating a Marxist revolutionary army that would redistribute wealth. Eventually, fighters used kidnapping, killing and the drug trade to fuel the insurgency, and the conflict became a war among leftist guerrillas, right-wing paramilitaries and a government backed by billions of dollars from Washington.

At the heart of the 2016 deal was a promise by FARC fighters to lay down their arms, and by the government to build institutions and fund programs that would eliminate the structural inequalities that caused the war.

It was an extremely ambitious promise: An oft-cited statistic from one international development organization is that it takes 11 generations for a Colombian family to rise out of poverty.

2016

FARC guerrillas at a camp deep in the Colombian jungle, months before the peace deal was finally ratified.

Daniela, a young FARC fighter, during a formation.

A FARC fighter known as El Primo riding a mule across the Quiparadó River in a remote stretch of jungle between the departments of Chocó and Antioquia.

A decade in, many changes are tangible: The vast majority of FARC fighters have not returned to arms — 85 percent remain in a program meant to reintegrate them into society, according to the United Nations. People traveling the highways outside Bogotá or Medellín generally do not fear kidnapping or bombs. Tourism flourishes in places once torn by conflict.

The government, at least in some places, has arrived in long-ignored towns with roads, schools and hospitals. The country has seen the opening of a vast new political space to debate something other than security, including social and economic issues, enriching public debate in a way that many feel is irreversible.

For decades the Colombian left struggled to distance itself from the violent guerrilla insurgency; distanced from that stigma, it won the presidency for the first time in 2022.

But Colombia’s violence did not disappear. Instead, it rearranged itself. The map of armed actors, each often competing to take over the criminal economies left by the FARC, is more dizzying than ever, and is supercharged by new technologies. TikTok and Facebook are used to recruit child soldiers. Hobby drones fitted with grenades are increasingly a weapon of choice.

Rebel fighters gathered for the last time before the peace agreement ending their 52-year insurgency.

President Juan Manuel Santos, left, speaking after the signing of the peace deal. FARC leaders sit on the opposite side of the stage and two, Iván Márquez and Jesús Santrich, later returned to arms.

FARC rebels in a camp before the deal was ratified.

FARC members who never signed the deal, or rearmed, have splintered into dissident factions. The National Liberation Army, or ELN, a Marxist group that never signed an accord, persists. One of the most powerful groups, known as the Clan del Golfo, is present in almost half of the country’s municipalities, according to Colombia’s ombudsman’s office, while FARC dissidents have a presence in more than a third.

The illicit economies that fed the war have been inherited, franchised and expanded. Production of the coca leaf, a key ingredient in cocaine, is up 80 percent since the accord was signed, according to the United Nations, and Colombia continues to be the world’s largest cocaine producer. For criminal groups, illegally mined gold is a growing part of the financial portfolio.

Some who remain in arms say they are still fighting for social justice.

“Colombia’s problem will be resolved when we resolve need and inequality,” said Andrey Avendaño, a FARC dissident commander, during an interview in a remote palm grove this year.

2018

Some FARC fighters resisted the deal, while others rearmed. Here, dissident guerrillas taught a member how to use his rifle at their camp, hidden among mountains north of Medellín.

The government, which had promised to sweep into lands once held by the FARC and bring health, education and potable water, was still largely absent in many places in 2018.

A group of fighters who didn’t sign the peace deal having breakfast by a mountain creek in Colombia.

But increasingly, fighting has become a profession, with ideology as window dressing. The FARC never paid a salary; when we visited a new armed group, the Comandos de la Frontera, in 2022, it paid twice the minimum wage — and offered vacation time.

Since taking office in August, Mr. De La Espriella has called the accord a failure, saying the agreement amounted to impunity for perpetrators. He has ended peace negotiations with remaining groups, intensified a military approach to the conflict, and proposed an antiterror law that would expand his powers to target enemies.

The United States, long one of the peace deal’s chief backers, has shifted its focus to this militarized, anti-narcotics approach, part of a larger strategy across the region.

Representatives for Mr. De La Espriella declined to comment for this article.

Scholars and everyday Colombians say his election reflects impatience with the pace of change.

2022

Members of the Comandos de la Frontera, a militia group that formed after the peace deal. Colombian officials said that by 2022 the number of armed groups in the country had grown to more than 30.

A militia member bathing in the Putumayo River.

Militia members on a patrol along the Putumayo river.

A comprehensive land reform meant to address a main driver of the conflict — unequal access to land — set a goal of distributing 3 million hectares to Colombians in need. About a tenth of that has been distributed, according to a United Nations Verification Mission.

Development programs in violence-affected areas were supposed to drive economic change. While 65 percent of programs are on an implementation track, only 5 to 10 percent of them were actually in place in areas recently studied by the ombudsman’s office.

A new court established by the deal, called the Special Jurisdiction for Peace, was one of the accord’s most symbolic and controversial aspects. Charged with investigating wrongdoing, it would mete out non-prison sentences, like hard labor, to those who admitted their crimes.

The court has uncovered the scope of many systematic crimes — establishing that the FARC kidnapped over 21,000 people and recruited nearly 19,000 children. And nearly 8,000 civilians were killed by the military and passed off as rebels in a scheme called the False Positives scandal.

Members of the Comandos de la Frontera militia pay cash for locally produced coca paste, a substance that is a midpoint in the production of cocaine.

A group of Comandos fighters packed and sealed their weapons before leaving camp for vacation, labeling them with their aliases: “Mincho,” “Max,” “Escorpión.”

2023

A member of a FARC dissident faction taking photos of a helicopter carrying United Nations personnel. Women made up an estimated 30 to 40 percent of the FARC’s fighters before the peace agreement.

But it has taken years to issue sentences, heightening a sense of impunity.

Just 27 percent of Colombians trust the court today, according to a study from the University of the Andes, down 10 percent from two years before.

Overall support for the agreement was just above 40 percent in 2016, and fell to about 37 percent last year.

A decade in, the nation debates the reasons violence persists.

Iván Duque, a conservative who opposed the deal, oversaw its early implementation. Critics accuse him of slow-walking the rollout of social programs and other measures, creating an institutional vacuum in rural areas in the first critical years.

Others fault the policies of his successor, leftist President Gustavo Petro, who favored negotiation with remaining groups over military operations, but failed to close any meaningful new deals.

Mr. Duque has blamed the end of a program that killed coca crops by dropping chemicals from planes, saying it allowed drugs to flourish. Mr. Petro has said he fast-tracked land reform after the country lost time under Mr. Duque.

2025

A gathering of dissident FARC fighters and community members in the Llanos del Yarí, a remote region of south central Colombia. In 2016, FARC fighters voted here to lay down their arms. Since then, those who rejected the peace deal have returned to this place again and again.

This gathering took place under President Petro, who tried unsuccessfully to strike peace deals with remaining armed groups.

Members of the post-2016 FARC patrol a rural area in the department of Caquetá.

In the territories most affected by violence, some remain skeptical of the deal, while others insist that a decade is not enough to judge a process devised to last generations.

And pain persists.

Deisy Dorelly Guanaro was 10 when FARC fighters took her from her mother’s home. She was sexually abused by commanders for years, she said, and rescued by the military after a battle in which she was the only survivor of 15 young fighters.

She criticized the accord’s truth and reconciliation process, saying perpetrators had not fully admitted their crimes and had received light punishments and even positions in Congress. The deal gave former FARC leaders seats in the legislature for two terms.

“I do not feel compensated for my pain,” Ms. Dorelly said, “or what they did to me when I was a child.”

2026

A guerrilla fighter, part of a dissident FARC unit, launching a drone at one of the rebels’ strategic positions in Catatumbo, on the border with Venezuela. Access to relatively cheap and easily modifiable drones is upending the country’s decades-long war against insurgent groups.

Locals riding through a town in Catatumbo, on the border with Venezuela, earlier this year. Graffiti celebrates the FARC and a poster calls for “armed rebellion.”

Andrey Avendaño, commander of the 33rd Front, a FARC dissident group that rejects the 2016 peace deal.

Perhaps the most Colombian feature of this anniversary is the sense that every peace agreement opens a new chapter of negotiation rather than closing one.

“One thing this agreement did was create this very broad political consensus that this violence doesn’t come from nowhere,” said Elizabeth Dickinson, deputy director for Latin America at International Crisis Group who is based in Colombia. “The fundamental conclusion is: You have to fix the lack of state presence, you have to provide services to people, you have to govern in these spaces, because otherwise someone else will.”

The 33rd Front has been fighting the ELN, a Colombian group that has grown significantly in recent years, in part because it has found refuge in neighboring Venezuela.

Members of the 33rd Front sleeping in their tent in a clandestine camp in the jungle.

A member of the 33rd Front.

The pact with the FARC did not resolve Colombia’s war. It resolved one war, the oldest and the most symbolic, and left on the table a map of lesser conflicts and illegal economies that the state still does not know how to confront, much less dismantle.

Colombia’s peace was never an endpoint but an unfinished process, subject to the shifting winds of each new government. The current president has inherited that ambiguity: an agreement that has survived against all odds, but that is still waiting, in the hardest-hit corners of the country, to accomplish the peace it promised on paper.

The ELN and dissident FARC groups cast themselves as protectors of the poor and refuse to lay down arms.

item.title: Dozens Unaccounted for After Fire Rips Through Candy Factory in Indonesia
item.description:
Two days after an inferno tore through a candy factory in Indonesia, leaving dozens of workers unaccounted for, firefighters were still cooling the charred debris in the two-storied building on Monday, worried that fires might reignite.

The blaze started on Saturday afternoon and raged for hours at the facility in Serang, Banten Province, about 50 kilometers, or 30 miles, from the capital, Jakarta. Initially the authorities said that three deaths had been confirmed, but later said that they needed to identify victims. Rescue workers had collected the remains of victims in two dozen body bags.

The factory, owned by the company Fonusa Agung Mulia, made milk candies and lollipops sold under the Milkita brand. The company said 300 people were inside the factory compound on Saturday, with 65 believed to be in the area where the fire broke out.

Rescue workers in masks were seen carrying black body bags out of the destroyed structure, whose roof had partially caved in. According to officials, 26 bags containing human remains were sent to hospitals for identification so far. The police on Monday said that 33 family members had provided DNA samples.

Said Iqbal, an adviser to President Prabowo Subianto, visited the site on Monday afternoon. In a statement, he said that the authorities were investigating whether a short circuit in the building’s air conditioning system triggered the fire. He also raised questions about the availability of escape routes.

Andra Soni, the governor of Banten Province, said emergency workers had not been able to access all parts of the factory. “Firefighting efforts are continuing in several sectors,” Mr. Soni said by telephone.

Television images showed the workers’ distressed relatives outside the factory, waiting for information about their loved ones. The fire also charred vehicles parked outside.

Firefighters fought the blaze for hours and were only able to get it under control around 6.30 a.m. on Sunday, according to Fonusa Agung Mulia, which is a subsidiary of Unifam.

The company’s chief executive, Steven Wijaya, apologized to the victims’ families during a news conference on Sunday. “We take full responsibility and are committed to helping the families, as well as our employees, get through this challenging period,” he said. “After all, our employees are part of our own family.”

The Association of All Indonesian Workers Unions called for an inquiry. “I don’t want to pre-empt the investigation by declaring the company negligent,” the group’s president, Mirah Sumirat, said in a statement on Monday. “However, when a fire results in loss of life and workers are still unaccounted for, the company’s entire safety system must be thoroughly examined.”

“This episode should not be viewed merely as a disaster or an unexpected accident,” Ms. Sumirat added. Companies needed to do “more than just completing administrative paperwork, installing safety signs or obtaining certification.”

Concerns about workplace safety in Indonesia are not new. Last December, 22 people died when a fire started in the office of a drone manufacturer. An explosion at a nickel-processing plant killed at least 13 people in 2023.

item.title: Ukraine Claims Strikes on Russian Ships Near Libya
item.description:
President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine said on Monday that Ukrainian forces were responsible for strikes on two Russian ships off the coast of Libya the previous day.

The strikes, near the port of Benghazi in eastern Libya, were the latest in an intensifying Ukrainian campaign against Russian vessels and showed that Ukraine’s reach extends even to the distant Mediterranean Sea.

Seven Ukrainian-made naval drones were deployed in the strikes, Mr. Zelensky said in a post on social media. One ship, a Russian corvette, sank, and a Russian combat helicopter was destroyed along with it, according to Mr. Zelensky. Ukraine also hit a Russian dry cargo vessel that he said was being used to transport weapons.

Satellite images showed a capsized Russian corvette. Mr. Zelensky also posted video of the attacks on the two ships. There was no immediate comment from the Russian authorities.

Mr. Zelensky did not say how Ukraine was able to get the naval drones, which are essentially exploding remote-controlled speedboats, into the Mediterranean. In previous strikes on Russian ships, Kyiv has often used aerial drones.

“We are responding to Russia’s aggression,” Mr. Zelensky said in his post. “We are developing Ukrainian weapons.”

The attack off the coast of Libya came a day after a Russian cargo ship, the Sparta II, was struck in the Gulf of Finland, in the eastern Baltic Sea. Ukraine has not claimed responsibility for that strike, but is believed to have been behind it. The Finnish prime minister also said his country supported Kyiv’s right to conduct such strikes.

A handful of Russian ships have been attacked, with both aerial and sea drones, in the Mediterranean over the past year or so. Ukraine has not acknowledged those strikes but is believed to have been behind at least some, or perhaps all, of them.

Mr. Zelensky’s statement on Monday was the first official acknowledgment of a Ukrainian sea-drone attack on Russian vessels in the Mediterranean.

The U.N. mission in Libya condemned the latest strikes and warned “against escalatory actions or rhetoric that could fuel tensions within Libya or draw the country into wider regional or international confrontations.”

“Libya cannot afford, and must not become, a battleground for foreign conflicts,” the mission said in a statement on Sunday.

item.title: Over 700,000 Russian Soldiers Have Died in Ukraine, Analysis Indicates
item.description:
More than 700,000 Russian soldiers have been killed in the war in Ukraine, according to a new estimate released on Monday, underscoring the extraordinary level of suffering that President Vladimir V. Putin has been willing to accept to pursue his war aims.

The updated estimate was calculated by the exiled Russian publications Meduza and Mediazona, making use of a trove of new data that two groups of pro-Ukraine hackers obtained from the Russian state statistics service, Rosstat. The groups, the Cyber Partisans of Belarus and Silent Crow, released the data to media outlets in recent weeks.

The estimate represents a significant increase from prior assessments of how many soldiers Russia has lost in the war. The Kremlin has concealed that information from the Russian public, leaving many Russians with only a cursory understanding of the scale of the death at the front.

Mr. Putin has been waging a full-scale war against Ukraine for nearly five years and does not appear ready to end it anytime soon. Armed with a powerful combination of repression, censorship and propaganda, the Russian leader has kept a lid on critical information about the war at home and dampened societal discontent about its high cost.

For years, Meduza and Mediazona have been tracking Russian war deaths, primarily by analyzing Russian probate records and death notices. The hack added significant new sources to their analysis, including data from Russia’s civil registry and government-run data exchange system, which feed anonymized information to Rosstat to inform national statistics.

Based on that new information, the publications identified at least 490,000 soldier deaths recorded by the Russian state as of September. But deaths regularly show up in the Russian government system with a huge time lag. The data, for instance, does not account for most of the deaths in 2026 and many from 2025.

Drawing on scientific projection methods, the publications came up with an estimate for what the death toll would be if the registrations were entirely up-to-date and included people who were listed as missing but were most likely dead.

The projection found that Russia had likely lost more than 700,000 soldiers killed, a significant increase from estimates that the publications released earlier this year. The projection did not address how many soldiers had been wounded.

The New York Times did not independently confirm the data or the analysis. Exact death counts during wars are very difficult to ascertain, with historians often disagreeing about casualty numbers for years after a conflict.

Michael Kofman, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, said that while Russia was losing more soldiers than it was recruiting, Moscow was still on track to recruit about 409,000 soldiers in 2026. The Russian authorities are still offering significant pay incentives for recruits.

The pace of recruiting allows Russia to sustain losses and keep fighting, but probably not to improve its position on the battlefield, Mr. Kofman said. Eventually, the Kremlin could find itself without sufficient assault infantry.

He said if Russia doesn’t change how its force is employed, it will continue to face “diminishing returns, with no prospect for improvement.”

There is relatively little reliable information in the public domain about Ukrainian losses. It is generally accepted that Russia has lost far more soldiers than Ukraine has, because armies attempting to advance almost always suffer significantly greater casualties. Russia has also employed tactics that military experts say have increased its battlefield toll.

The Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington estimated that 150,000 Ukrainian combatants had died in the war through June. Two opaque websites that track public information about Ukrainian deaths, Lostarmour.info and UALosses.org, put the number of Ukrainian soldiers lost and missing at well over 200,000.

Alina Lobzina contributed reporting.

item.title: They Were Too Old to Enlist, but Not to Fight. Meet the Steppe Wolves of Ukraine.
item.description:
They called themselves pioneers, which they thought sounded better than pensioners. It was age, after all, that had gotten them rejected by the Ukrainian military and forced to find another way to join the fight for survival against Russia.

“No one can forbid me, at any age, from defending my country, my land, and my family,” said one of the men, whose call sign — naturally enough — is Grandpa. “If they won’t accept us officially, we’ll do it unofficially.”

Grandpa, who got his call sign before he actually had any grandchildren, was 65 when Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. At the time, Ukraine’s army was accepting only soldiers age 60 and under, so he formed a group of partisans known as the Steppe Wolves.

The outfit fought near Melitopol, then Vasylivka and later Kamianske. These days, they number about a dozen and are primarily based in the Zaporizhzhia region.

That is where, on a visit one early spring afternoon, we saw camouflage pants hanging on a clothesline outside the nondescript building that served as their base. Inside, dozens of rockets were stacked on the floor, many in various states of disrepair.

Ukrainian military units from all over have brought faulty rockets to the Steppe Wolves, who repair them in exchange for being able to keep some for their own use. They have also refurbished abandoned rockets they found to use against Russian positions. Ukrainian soldiers send them coordinates and targets for those strikes, and in some cases even provide additional ammunition.

One artillery commander in a Ukrainian military special operations unit said that he had worked with the Steppe Wolves since 2022 and that they were far more than just enthusiasts.

“They don’t just help with moral support or kind words,” the commander, whose call sign is Bush, said in a phone interview. The older soldiers carry out missions, he said, describing them as “very mobile” as well as “fast and effective.”

Bush, who like the others soldiers interviewed asked to be identified only by his call sign, in keeping with military protocol, said he would gladly bring the Steppe Wolves into his unit officially.

“Judging by age isn’t right,” he said. “It’s about motivation.” And the Steppe Wolves, he said, “just want to work.”

At the Steppe Wolves base one cold morning, a soldier who goes by the name Dnipro, 64, was repairing a detonator in a cramped workshop that smelled like gunpowder. He needs glasses to drive but otherwise has no physical limitations, he said.

“We don’t feel old,” Dnipro said. “Not young, of course — but not old either.”

Like many of his comrades, Dnipro argued that his age made him an asset. “With age everyone gains experience,” he said, pointing to his years of mechanical work and ability to work in teams.

Arsen, 66, used to work as a welder making boilers in Kharkiv. After Russia invaded in 2022, he said, he went to a recruitment office but was told he was “not needed.”

When his son joined the military in January 2024, Arsen said, he was worried, but also proud to see his child “defending the Motherland, not hiding behind his wife’s skirt.”

Six months later, his son was dead.

Arsen spent half a year in deep grief, avoiding life and people, he said, until he realized he “had to do something.” That “something” was serving his country, which led to the Steppe Wolves.

His wife was not pleased, at least initially. Her position later softened, he said, recalling how she told him “go — I understand.”

“My son fought for me. Now I fight for him,” Arsen said. “There was no other decision.”

He said he planned to stay with the Steppe Wolves as long as his health allowed. He has no limitations yet, he said, aside from needing reading glasses.

“Here I found my brothers,” he said that chilly spring afternoon. “And here I feel that I am in my place.”

Petro, 68, insisted that he was “still young.” A former professional weight lifter and coach, he walked with arms held out from his sides like a man who pumps serious iron.

“Now it is especially important to keep my physical condition, because the rockets are heavy,” he explained one morning after lifting weights at a nearby gym.

The only difference between him and a regular soldier, Petro said, was that “we don’t get paid.”

“If, for example, I die, my family won’t receive anything,” he said. “No social protection. Nothing. That’s just the reality.”

He spoke without bitterness, saying he fought not for money but out of duty. But a bit of recognition, he conceded, would be nice.

A month earlier, with Ukraine stricken by troop shortages, President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine had signed a decree that would allow anyone over 60 to serve with a one-year contract in the military, with the possibility to extend. But it was taking time for that to trickle down, and in the meantime the Steppe Wolves were in limbo.

“Deep down, it’s a bit hurtful that we’ve put in so much effort and they still can’t organize us properly,” Petro said, as an air-raid warning started to wail. “But the most important thing is to drive the enemy out of here.”

Eventually, he and the other men got their wish: one-year contracts with Ukraine’s military.

The men of the Steppe Wolves were now official.

item.title: Drone Attack Hits Colombian City as Unmanned Explosives Transform Conflict
item.description:
Drones launched explosives that destroyed a home in a major Colombian city on Monday morning in the first such attack inside a major population hub, as the cheap devices reshape a conflict between the country’s armed groups and the military.

The drones injured three people in the city of Cúcuta, according to George Quintero, a retired colonel who now works as a security adviser to the regional government. He added that they were most likely launched by one of two armed groups battling for control of illicit economies.

The Colombian military, with financial and technical help from the United States, has long fought armed insurgencies and criminal groups. In the last two years, readily accessible commercial drones fitted with explosives have given armed groups new ways to attack government forces and terrorize the population.

Until now, those strikes have happened in relatively rural areas.

The attack on Monday occurred at about 3 a.m., Colonel Quintero said in an interview with the Colombian radio station Blu Radio. The worst-damaged home is half a block away from a police station, which may have been the target of the attack. More than 60 homes and businesses were affected by the explosives, the colonel said, which shattered windows and left shrapnel in walls.

The United Nations reported that drone bombings have risen to 333 instances in 2025 from 61 in 2024, a 445 percent increase.

Cúcuta is on the border with Venezuela, in a region of vast fields of coca, a base ingredient in cocaine. For the last two years, two armed groups — the National Liberation Army, or ELN, and the 33rd Front, a splinter group of the former Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia — have been battling for control of the territory. Thousands of people have been displaced by the violence, and many others have been killed.

The area and the two groups have been major military targets for Colombia’s new right-wing president, Abelardo De La Espriella, as well as for the Trump administration, which has been focused on armed groups and illicit economies across Latin America. Last month, in a region on the Colombia-Venezuela border to the south of Cúcuta, the United States assisted the Venezuelan government in an attack on the ELN.

Asked on Blu Radio whether the Colombian government had the right technology to fight the drone attacks, Colonel Quintero said that “there is currently no magic wand anywhere in the world that can effectively counter it.”

“The current national government has provided some tools — such as anti-drone guns and other specialized equipment — and additional procurement is underway,” he added.

But several strikes had taken place in rural areas just as the assault in Cúcuta was underway.

“There were another five this morning,” he said. “It is extremely complex to achieve full coverage against this type of drone-based attack.”

On Monday morning in Cúcuta, explosives had destroyed one home and damaged others. Glass from blown-out windows littered the street.

“The bomb fell right on top of the house,” said Orlando Roa, who said he had escaped the attack with his wife and 17-month-old son. He had shrapnel lodged in his leg, he said. His wife and son seemed to be all right but were being examined at a hospital.

“Thank God they were protected,” he said.

Federico Rios contributed reporting from Cúcuta, Colombia.

item.title: Netanyahu Wants to Attack Iran. Does That Serve Israel or Him?
item.description:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s all-out push for a new Israeli military strike against Iran is being called into question by critics who say that it cannot be disentangled from his efforts to maintain his grip on power.

The embattled Israeli leader, now serving in a caretaker role, has personally lobbied President Trump and sent emissaries to make the case to White House, C.I.A. and U.S. Central Command officials for a new attack on Iran, officials briefed on the discussions have said. But Mr. Netanyahu has yet to tell his own citizens why that would be necessary now, what it would achieve or how it could be contained without escalating into a regional conflagration.

Even analysts who tend to trust the warnings emanating from the Israeli intelligence and military establishment say that it is unclear whether a fresh round of attacks would serve Israel’s interests — or Mr. Netanyahu’s.

“It’s very difficult to make a distinction between the political considerations and the urgency of the threats,” said Raz Zimmt, head of Iran research at the Institute for National Security Studies in Tel Aviv. The chatter among Israeli security officials, he said, suggested a growing consensus that pre-emptive military action would become necessary before long, as Iran’s offensive capabilities grow into greater threats. But there was no such consensus about when.

“Whether it really requires an immediate action? I doubt it,” Mr. Zimmt said.

The belief that Mr. Netanyahu would stop at almost nothing to stay in power has made it difficult for many Israelis to take his word about the necessity of an attack, let alone about the need to execute one immediately.

“For the sake of his political survival, Netanyahu is pushing Israel into another war,” said Yair Golan, the leader of the left-wing Democrats party and a former deputy chief of staff of the Israeli military. “A government responsible for the gravest security failure in the country’s history, and for a string of strategic security failures, has no legitimacy whatsoever to launch another military campaign.”

Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief who has been given a chance to form a new government, told Israelis on Friday that Mr. Netanyahu was risking their security.

“The fact that operational interests and timetables are being conflated with political interests and agendas — and that this has become completely normalized — is unacceptable,” he wrote in a post on social media. “It is madness and a source of danger.”

A spokesman for the prime minister, Doron Spielman, denied that political calculations factored into Mr. Netanyahu’s approach to Iran.

“The prime minister’s decisions on Iran are guided by one consideration: the security of Israel and its citizens,” Mr. Spielman said in a statement. “Iran’s regime openly threatens Israel, the United States, Europe and the West, and is working to acquire the means to carry out those threats. That threat does not run on a political calendar.”

It is unclear whether Israel would be willing to attack Iran on its own, or if it would do so provided it had U.S. approval and assurances of support in the event of an Iranian counterstrike.

Three Israeli security officials said that the Israeli military’s position — as presented in internal discussions, including with the prime minister — was that if the opportunity arose to strike alongside the United States, Israel should take it. Israeli officials are aware that the opportunity could close in January, when Democrats take control of the U.S. Congress.

However, the three officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive matters, said that the view among many senior Israeli commanders was that Israel must not, in the near term, launch an attack on its own. That would risk squandering the opportunity of a joint strike. And the officials said that the consensus was that there was no urgency and no reason for Israel to attack alone.

Any immediate action could benefit Mr. Netanyahu politically — by disrupting Mr. Eisenkot’s efforts to form a government before a Dec. 6 deadline, and by creating public pressure for a national unity government that included Mr. Netanyahu.

A joint U.S.-Israel attack on Iran might even prompt Mr. Trump to throw his weight behind a potential unity government, some Israeli analysts have speculated.

Even before the Oct. 27 election, as polls predicted defeat for the prime minister, The New York Times reported that Mr. Netanyahu hoped to renew fighting with Iran to generate pressure on Mr. Eisenkot to enter an emergency unity government.

Now, after flatly ruling out a unity government during his campaign, Mr. Netanyahu has been seeding the airwaves with talk of a unity government for nearly two weeks.

Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition had a poor showing in the election. Opposition parties won 67 seats in the 120-seat Parliament. In the days that followed, the prime minister first tried to cast doubt on the integrity of the vote, then sought to deter the opposition from forming a government that relied on the support of predominantly Arab parties, which won a record 19 seats.

But on Nov. 7, he and his allies abruptly began beating the drum for a unity government, arguing that Israel’s Jewish political parties should come together — centrist and left-wing factions joining his right-wing bloc — to “remove the nuclear threat from Iran, preserve Israel as a Jewish state and bring unity among us,” as Mr. Netanyahu put it.

Two days later, he added a key point: “The one who should lead this government, naturally, is the largest party,” he said.

That would be his party, Likud, which won 27 seats in Parliament.

Not surprisingly, there were no takers among the opposition parties, led by Mr. Eisenkot, whose Yashar party won 21 seats. The most adamant of all Mr. Eisenkot’s campaign promises was that Mr. Netanyahu would be dislodged from the premiership.

Resuming the fighting with Iran, however, could amount to the kind of national emergency that tests the resolve of Mr. Eisenkot and his allies to refuse Mr. Netanyahu’s overtures. There is a recent precedent: Mr. Eisenkot entered a unity government led by Mr. Netanyahu after the Hamas-led attacks of Oct. 7, 2023.

Already on Wednesday and Thursday, Mr. Netanyahu arranged briefings on the security situation for two of Mr. Eisenkot’s key allies, Naftali Bennett, a former prime minister who leads the Beyachad (Together) party, and Avigdor Liberman of the Yisrael Beiteinu (Our Home) party.

Mr. Bennett has said he favors a unity government, but one led by Mr. Eisenkot, at least to start. Mr. Liberman has rejected any unity government with Mr. Netanyahu, calling it a “trap” and saying that “even if the world turns upside down, I won’t sit with Netanyahu.”

Analysts point to those differences as evidence that Mr. Netanyahu’s unity gambit is working, by stoking friction within Mr. Eisenkot’s bloc. If Mr. Eisenkot and his allies fail to form a government, the likely result would be new elections, in which Mr. Netanyahu would be expected to fare better than in last month’s vote.

Suspicions about Mr. Netanyahu’s motives in national-security matters have clouded his current four-year term as prime minister, and were a factor again when he began pushing to attack Iran before the election.

He met resistance at the time from within the armed forces, including from the military chief of staff, Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir, who objected to a strike during the run-up to the vote because of the political sensitivities and the difficulty of explaining to the public why an attack had to occur then.

Israel’s goals in a possible strike against Iran have not been detailed publicly by Mr. Netanyahu, but security officials and analysts point to a few potential objectives.

Israel’s military considers intelligence about Iran’s chemical weapons program most concerning in the short term, according to two Israeli security officials, though it is unclear whether such weapons could be deployed soon.

Other possible justifications include further attempts to damage Iran’s nuclear program or its ballistic missile and drone arsenal, which experts say Iran has been replenishing.

An attack on Iran’s energy infrastructure is another possibility, security officials say, should the United States and Israel choose to make a new attempt at precipitating regime change in Tehran.

At the height of the war, the United States and Israel struck civilian infrastructure in Iran that the Iranian authorities said included roads, bridges, rail lines and schools. Israel also attacked Iranian petrochemical and storage sites.

Iran retaliated by attacking U.S. allies in the Gulf. Those countries said they were hit by thousands of missiles and drones targeting energy facilities, airports and water and power plants. Iranian missiles struck apartment buildings and at least one railway station in Israel, the authorities there said.

But Israel planned a wider strike — against Iranian oil production, refining and global export infrastructure, as well as other critical infrastructure in the country — as part of a plan to topple the regime. Mr. Trump put a halt to it.

Later on, however, Mr. Trump threatened similar strikes, saying they would lead to the “destruction of Iranian civilization.”

Destroying such civilian infrastructure would cause widespread suffering in a country of 93 million people and in most cases would be considered a war crime under international law.

Now, those plans are back on the table, according to the three Israeli security officials.

Iran has vowed to respond to such a strike by retaliating against oil facilities, water desalination plants, data centers and other civilian infrastructure across the region, defying hopes of containing a renewed conflict.

Adam Rasgon and Natan Odenheimer contributed reporting from Tel Aviv.
